changed_views: Subagent proliferation can be a cost problem rather than an automatic performance benefit: Warp reports gains from reducing redundant work and choosing less expensive models for bounded steps.
A factory's definition, traces and task suites can become engineering assets of their own, but proposing a workflow change and validating that it improves outcomes remain distinct steps.

Infrastructure that preserves customers' model commitments offers a different commercial position from reselling coding-agent inference; the episode does not establish Warp's resulting margins or customer returns.
follow_ups: Request the period, task mix, PR counts, complete cost coverage and human-review effort behind the $80 to $15–20 and 40% throughput comparisons.
Look for representative held-out suites, repetitions, uncertainty and expert checks of correctness grading before trusting the internal model trade-off.
Track whether proposed factory changes receive replay-based validation, how regressions are caught, and who approves deployment.
Compare implementation effort and total platform cost across small teams, standard startup stacks and enterprises with bespoke infrastructure.

signals.claim: Lloyd reports Warp reduced cost per PR from about $80 to $15–20 by changing model choices and reducing redundant subagents.
signals.evidence: He says expensive models were used for tasks such as triage and too many subagents duplicated work. After tuning, he reports the lower cost, 40% more PR throughput over the previous month and no increase in revert rate. He does not disclose task mix, sample size or whether the throughput comparison counts opened or merged PRs. [Warp's current metric documentation](https://docs.warp.dev/factories/measure-and-improve/) defines cost per PR as median estimated cost per opened PR, including child runs, and warns about historical estimates and incomplete external-inference coverage. The interview does not establish that historical calculation method or a reduction in total engineering cost; revert rate is a limited quality measure.

signals.claim: Warp uses internal task suites to compare both models and harnesses, making routing decisions specific to a team's codebase.
signals.evidence: Lloyd describes curating prior agent runs and replaying tasks across configurations. In one displayed internal task set, he reports one configuration at 95% correctness and $6 average cost, versus another at 93% and $2. Those are task-run comparisons, not per-PR costs or general coding scores; suite size, uncertainty and independent grader validation are absent. [The benchmark documentation](https://docs.warp.dev/factories/benchmarks/) specifies fixed tasks for one factory agent, explicit correctness criteria and repeated trials. The supported conclusion is a method for testing local cost-quality trade-offs, not a universal model ranking.

signals.claim: Code-defined workflows let Warp's agents propose fixes to repeated failures, but replay-based validation of each proposed fix was still future work.
signals.evidence: Lloyd shows a YAML factory definition, stored conversations and artifacts, and configurable LLM graders that can retrospectively classify failures. A displayed example identifies 54 triage failures and proposes allowing the triage agent to delegate investigation. Coding agents can open a PR against the factory definition. He explicitly says automatically replaying the old runs to verify that each proposed change helps is not yet available. The loop produces inspectable proposals; the interview does not establish autonomous acceptance or proven improvement of those proposals.

signals.claim: Warp positions Factories as infrastructure for optimizing coding agents, with inference and harness choice intended to fit customers' existing commitments.
signals.evidence: Lloyd says companies want to use existing Anthropic, OpenAI or Google commitments, and describes bringing an inference provider and ACP-compatible harness instead of relying entirely on Warp's stack. He argues that selling only a coding agent has difficult economics and instead pitches optimization and productivity infrastructure. He also says small teams may find the factory excessive and highly bespoke enterprises require implementation work. [Current pricing](https://www.warp.dev/pricing) labels Factories Early Access and reserves some controls for Enterprise; the interview's flexibility claim should not be read as universal feature access or an entirely open-source platform.

summary: Warp CEO Zach Lloyd describes a software factory defined in code, with shared agent traces, configurable graders and benchmarks on internal tasks. He reports reducing Warp's cost per PR from about $80 to $15–20 by changing models and reducing redundant subagents, alongside a 40% increase in PR throughput over the previous month and an unchanged revert rate. The demo shows agents proposing changes to the factory definition; automatic replay to validate each proposed change is explicitly still planned. Warp's strategy is to sell the infrastructure for operating and improving coding agents, while supporting multiple models and harnesses. The reported outcomes lack a controlled comparison or a complete accounting of engineering costs.
why_it_matters: The strongest mechanism is making the workflow itself measurable and editable: representative tasks can reveal cheaper configurations, while retained traces expose repeated failures. The business case depends on how accurately those measures reflect shipped quality and on integration costs, especially when comparing a shared platform with individual coding-agent subscriptions.
